questions.stem: A 33-year-old man presented with a 72-hour history of fever and malaise. He also had a mild headache and reported some loose stools and abdominal pain. He had returned 5 days earlier from a 6-week trip to Chad where he worked with locals to build a church. During the construction work, he was bitten by many mosquitoes. He also traveled throughout the region inspecting waterways. He had unprotected vaginal intercourse with 2 casual partners. He did not seek advice prior to his travels. On examination, his temperature was 39.3°C, his heart rate was 88 beats/minute, and his blood pressure was 120/68 mmHg. He was flushed with reddened conjunctivae. He had tender hepatomegaly of 2 cm below the costal margin. Investigations: Total WBC count 3.5 ×109/L Platelet count 150 ×109/L eGFR >60 mL/min/1.73 m2 Bilirubin 3 mg/dL AST 177 U/L ALT 89 U/L
questions.lead_in: What intervention would have prevented his condition?
questions.explanation: Yellow fever immunization This is yellow fever, within the first viremic stage of infection. This will be followed by a period of remission for up to 48 hours, and then a proportion of patients will develop the third life-threatening stage of intoxication. Yellow fever vaccine is recommended for patients (above the age of 9 months) who will travel to the Americas and sub-Saharan Africa. This live attenuated vaccine is not recommended for immunocompromised patients. Booster doses after 10 years are recommended to a subset of individuals who may be at continued risk. Malaria, viral hepatitis, and leptospirosis should be considered in the differential but the rash, the platelet count, and the normal renal function make them less likely than yellow fever. Antibiotic or antiparasitic prophylaxis may be recommended on certain geographic regions, but would not protect him against yellow fever. Hepatitis A, typhoid, and hepatitis B immunizations would all be appropriate to recommend to this man, but would not have protected him.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q28

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man was admitted with new onset confusion and a 2-day history of fevers. The fevers began during his return home from a month-long safari in South Africa. He was found to have severe P. falciparum malaria and treated with IV artesunate with significant improvement. Ten days later, he developed a sudden drop in hemoglobin and rise in bilirubin.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Artesunate hemolysis Delayed postartesunate hemolysis is likely the result of the clearance of previously infected erythrocytes by the spleen. Artesunate kills parasites while not affecting the erythrocytes themselves; however, their ultimate lifespan is shortened. This generally happens 7–14 days after treatment initiation.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q8

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man was admitted with a three-day history of abdominal pain and fevers. He lived in New York City, but recently traveled to visit family in Malaysia. He did not seek pretravel counseling. On physical examination, he appeared acutely ill. His blood pressure was 108/55 mmHg, his pulse rate was 114 beats/ minute, and his temperature was 40°C. He had abdominal tenderness and was dyspneic at rest, with increasing oxygen requirements. Investigations: Hemoglobin level 8.3 mmol/L Platelet count 56 ×109/L Peripheral white cell 4.5 ×109cells/L Blood smear revealed the following, with parasitemia to 3.8%.
questions.lead_in: What pathogen is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: P. knowlesi The patient has manifestations of severe malaria, with high parasitemia and end-organ damage. P. falciparum is the most common cause of severe malaria. However, you are shown a band trophozoite on peripheral smear. This is consistent with P. knowlesi. Another clue is geographic. This patient is in an area where P. knowlesi is present. It is important, especially for your boards, to be able to differentiate between malaria species. P. falciparum Banana Severe disease Schuffner dots Band trophozoite Severe disease Band trophozoite Mild disease Round or oval Can have Schuffner dots P. malariae P. ovale P. knowlesiP. vivax
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q17

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man developed fever and headache 1 week after returning from an 8-week holiday to South America. He had stayed in a retreat in the middle of the Amazon jungle. He did not seek travel advice before his travel and had not taken any malaria prophylaxis or travel vaccinations. He had stayed in a wood hut with palm leaf roof. He slept under a bednet, but he ran out of mosquito repellent. He had been well while there. His symptoms had persisted for 4 days before he sought medical attention. A fellow traveler had informed him that she had been diagnosed with malaria. On examination he was alert and oriented. His heart rate was 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/74 mmHg, temperature 37.1°C. He was thin, but there was no palpable lymphadenopathy or rash. Examination of his cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal systems was unremarkable. Investigations: Hemoglobin 114 g/L (130–180) Platelet count 137 ×109/L (150–400) Serum creatinine 74 μmol/L (60–110) Malaria antigen positive Malaria film: see image
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Chloroquine plus primaquine This is the recommended treatment of choice for P. vivax infection currently according to Public Health England. Primaquine is required to clear the hypnozoite stage of infection in order to prevent relapse. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q39

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man was admitted with a 6-day history of fever and chills. He had also noticed some shortness of breath while walking. Ten days earlier he had arrived in the United States from Myanmar. He had no prior medical history but had been depressed for the past year. On examination, he was awake, alert, and oriented. His temperature was 39.2°C, and his blood pressure was 110/58 mmHg. He had pale conjunctivae and some pitting edema to his ankles. Investigations: Hemoglobin 5.8 g/dL Total bilirubin 3.1 mg/mL Peripheral blood smear:
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: IV artesunate for 24 hours followed by atovaquone– proguanil for 3 days
IV artesunate for 24 hours followed by oral mefloquine for 3 days
IV artesunate to complete 3-day course of therapy

questions.explanation: IV artesunate for 24 hours followed by atovaquone– proguanil for 3 days The peripheral smear shows the presence of a Plasmodium falciparum gametocyte, classically described as “bananashaped” and ring trophozoites. Although the patient is hemodynamically stable, he has signs of severe malaria, including a hemoglobin <7 g/dL and a bilirubin >3 mg/mL. For that reason, the most appropriate therapy is IV therapy with artesunate followed by an oral agent. The IV therapy should be continued for a minimum of 24 hours and should be transitioned to an oral regimen to complete a full course of therapy. They also need to have a second agent to ensure eradication of parasites. The patient has a prior history of depression and mefloquine would be contraindicated as it is associated with neuropsychiatric disturbances. Given the emergence of resistance in the South Asian continent, chloroquine is no longer an acceptable option for this region. (From Garcia LS. Malaria. Clin Lab Med. 2010;30(1):93–129.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q18

questions.question: 17.  Severe malaria in Canadian traveller.  Has Hb 65. Sao2 of 85%. Confused and GCS 9. Falciparum parasitemia of 6%.

parts.text: A.  What criteria does he have for severe disease?
B.  What is the histopathologic feature of cerebral malaria?
C.  What are four other criteria for severe disease?
D.  What is the treatment?

cohort_answer.text:
Parasetemia >5% in non-immune for >5yo; Hb <70; ARDS; Impaired conciousness
Sequestration of infected RBCs in brain microvasculature, ring haemorrhages
IV artesunate for at least 24 hours then complete therapy with a course of atovaquone-proguanil

questions.question: The ED and community travel medicine clinic have approached you because they feel the thin smears done for malaria testing is insensitive.

parts.text: What are 2 issues to discuss with the ED/clinic to improve sensitivity?
Name 2 different tests for malaria detection. For each, give 1 disadvantage.

questions.model_answer: a) Issues to improve sensitivity of thin smears: (1) a single negative smear does not rule out malaria - repeat thick and thin smears every 12-24 hours x 3 sets before excluding the diagnosis, since parasitemia can be low/cyclical and mature P. falciparum forms sequester in microvasculature (2) ensure an experienced microscopist examines >=200-500 fields (thick smear read for ~20 minutes) as low-volume readers under-detect low parasitemia. b) Two other tests and a disadvantage of each: Rapid diagnostic test (HRP-2/pLDH antigen) - disadvantage: HRP-2 can remain positive for weeks after successful treatment (false positive for active infection) and gene deletions (pfhrp2/3) cause false negatives. PCR - disadvantage: not widely available at point of care, longer turnaround, higher cost, so not useful for immediate treatment decisions.
questions.cites: Mandell pp. 3301, 3312-3313 (thick/thin smear technique and RDT limitations)

questions.question: 29. Plasmodium knowlesi is a new species causing malaria in humans.

parts.text: Shortly describe how its morphology compares with other Plasmodium spp. on a blood smear
b) Name the geographic region where most cases have been acquired
c) Why is it important to make the difference between this species and other non-falciparum species?

cohort_answer.text: Morphology: Early trophozoites resemble P. falciparum, later erythrocytic stages resemble P. malariae, making microscopy alone difficult. High parasitemias (replicates q24hr vs q3d for P. malariae); infects RBC of all ages; RBC diameter normal (vs big RBC in P. vivax/ovale); no ameboid trophozoites; band forms present (key for P. malariae/P. knowlesi); up to 16 merozoites. Region: SE Asia (Malaysia). Importance: P. knowlesi infections have higher parasitemias and can cause severe disease, similar to P. falciparum.

questions.question: Patient who traveled to India and Cambodia. Malaria prophylaxis with Mefloquine. Sx severe malaria and positive rapid test when returning to Canada.

parts.text: Which Plasmodium species is most likely involved?
Explain why?
What is the place of acquisition?
Name two treatments (first and second line)
Explain why first-line treatment is better
How to monitor the potential emergence of resistance to first-line treatment?

cohort_answer.text:
Species: P. falciparum
Why: Falciparum & vivax sp are found in both countries but falciparum is the only one that typically causes severe malaria. Known mefloquine resistance in Cambodia.
Place of acquisition: Cambodia (has areas of Mefloquine resistance)
Treatments: Parentral Artesunate; Parentral Quinine + clinda
Why first-line better: Rapid activity, clears parasitemia faster; Activity against all erythrocytic stages of the parasite; Minimal resistance; Very well tolerated, less adverse effects compared to quinine (eg hypoglycaemia); Easy to administer; No dose adjustment for organ impairment; No significant drug interactions; Does not require cardiac monitoring. Disadvantages: Short half life <2hrs therefore can relapse if not given an oral course as step down; Can cause delayed haemolysis (weekly CBCs x 4 weeks)
Monitoring resistance: Repeat blood smears to monitor clearance of parasitemia – if delayed, may have resistance

parts.text: Malaria for rapid diagnosis list the following (2 for each): advantage, disadvantage for smear, RDT, and PCR.

cohort_answer.text: Smear - Advantage: Allows for quantification and speciation. Disadvantage: Need a trained technician/hematopathologist to read/do smear; Can be false negative if low level parasitemia. RDT - Advantage: Rapid results. Disadvantage: Doesn't provide quantification of parasitemia; Doesn't identify all malaria species. PCR - Advantage: High sensitivity and specificity for identification, can detect low parasitemias. Disadvantage: Not widely available; Expensive

questions.question: 7. 29yo patient, Canadian born, returns from West Africa with fever and dyspnea. GCS 9, fever, SpO2 85%, RR 30, Hb 65, GCS 9, parasitemia 6%.

parts.text: What are 4 criteria for severe malaria that are met by the patient

The patient has parasitemia of 2% on day 2, 1% on day 3. Do you consider this to be an adequate response to therapy?

cohort_answer.text: Criteria met: Parasitemia, GCS, Hgb, SpO2. Other criteria: Prostration, Bili >50, Glucose <2.2, pH <7.25. Histopathologic hallmark: Sequestration of RBCs in vessels, with extra-erythrocytic pigmentation and perivascular leukocytes. Treatment: Artemisinin derivative (IV). Adequate response: yes

questions.question: Malaria question

parts.text: First line therapy (generic) for vivax from Peru, uncomplicated falciparum from South Sudan, complicated malaria from South Sudan
4 clinical and 4 lab criteria for severe malaria

questions.model_answer: a) First-line therapy: vivax from Peru (chloroquine-sensitive region) - chloroquine plus primaquine (after G6PD testing) for radical cure. Uncomplicated falciparum from South Sudan (chloroquine-resistant) - artemether-lumefantrine (or another ACT). Complicated/severe falciparum from South Sudan - IV artesunate. b) Severe malaria criteria - Clinical (4): impaired consciousness/coma, respiratory distress/pulmonary edema, seizures (multiple), shock/circulatory collapse. Lab (4): parasitemia >5-10%, severe anemia (Hb <7 g/dL), hypoglycemia (<2.2 mmol/L), acute kidney injury (creatinine >3 mg/dL) or severe acidosis.

questions.question: How would you treat the following patients with malaria: Adult with uncomplicated P. vivax acquired in Peru; Adult with uncomplicated P. falciparum acquired in South Sudan; Adult with complicated P. falciparum acquired in South Sudan.

parts.text: Adult with uncomplicated P. vivax acquired in Peru - treatment?
Adult with uncomplicated P. falciparum acquired in South Sudan - treatment?
Adult with complicated P. falciparum acquired in South Sudan - treatment?
What are 4 clinical and 4 lab-based criteria for complicated malaria?

cohort_answer.text: P. vivax Peru: Malarone; Quinine + Doxycycline or clindamycin; Primaquine 30mg base for 14 days; screen for G6PD deficiency; monitor for drug-induced hemolysis. P. falciparum uncomplicated South Sudan: Atovaquone-proguanil PO x3 days. P. falciparum complicated South Sudan: IV artesunate 2.4mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 and 48h; follow on with atovaquone-proguanil x3 days starting 4h after final dose of artesunate; if received <4 doses artesunate, follow-on with 3 days atovaquone-proguanil or 7 days oral quinine+doxycycline/clindamycin; if received 4 full doses over 48hrs, follow-on can be 3 days atovaquone-proguanil, or 7 days doxycycline or 7 days clindamycin. 4 clinical/4 lab criteria for complicated malaria: not documented

questions.question: 17. Girl returns from Malawi and had been diagnosed with uncomplicated P. falciparum (mother brings you documentation). She was treated with 3 days of artemether-lumefantrine 10 days ago. Physician in community reorders RDT and smears. RDT returns positive. She is afebrile and well appearing and there was a smear with gametocytes of P. falciparum. Normal bw otherwise. No other plans to travel.

parts.text: 4 specific reasons why the RDT is positive
What is the recommended management now

questions.model_answer: a) Four reasons RDT remains positive 10 days post-treatment despite clinical cure: (1) persistent HRP-2 antigenemia, which can remain detectable for 2-4 weeks after adequate treatment even with parasite clearance (2) presence of circulating gametocytes (which do not indicate treatment failure - gametocytes can persist after asexual clearance) (3) true treatment failure/recrudescence (less likely given wellness and normal labs) (4) new/reinfection (excluded here as no further travel). b) Management: no retreatment needed - reassure and observe; RDT positivity from residual HRP-2 antigen and gametocytemia without symptoms does not represent treatment failure; repeat smear/RDT is not indicated given clinical well-being and no further exposure risk.
questions.cites: Mandell pp. 3312-3313 (RDT persistence and gametocyte biology)

questions.question: 24yo with recent travel to Malawi, reports he was treated 10 days ago there for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria with artemisinin-lumefantrine x 3 days. Feeling well.

parts.text: RDT is positive for P falciparum (no smear given). Give 4 reasons for this result.
Thick and thin smear shows only gametocytes for P falciparum, B/W otherwise normal apart from anemia. Would you treat again and give a reason. No travel planned in the next year.
Give two regimens for treating uncomplicated falciparum malaria available in Canada

questions.model_answer: a) Four reasons for positive RDT at day 10: (1) persistent HRP-2 antigenemia despite parasite clearance (can persist weeks) (2) residual circulating gametocytes (3) true recrudescence/treatment failure (4) reinfection (unlikely, no further travel). b) Would not retreat: gametocytes alone (without asexual forms) on smear with a well-appearing, otherwise normal patient reflects post-treatment gametocytemia, not treatment failure - gametocytes are not affected by most blood schizonticides and can persist for weeks without indicating ongoing infection or transmission risk to self. c) Two regimens for uncomplicated falciparum available in Canada: artemether-lumefantrine, and atovaquone-proguanil (quinine plus doxycycline is an alternative).

questions.question: Kid traveled in Africa, present with fever 39.5, RR30, sat 85%, parasitemia 6%, confusion/Glasgow 9

parts.text: 4 criteria of severe malaria in this case
4 other criteria of severe malaria
Best treatment
Parasitemia down to 2% at D2, 1% at D3. Do you consider this as therapeutic success

cohort_answer.text: 4 criteria of severe malaria in this case: Parasitemia 6% (in non-immune); Resp: SpO2 85%; GCS 9; ?confusion. Best treatment: IV artesunate. Therapeutic success: Yes

questions.question: Travel returning from India via Cambodia (stayed there several days – no clear timeline given during trip) had been on mefloquine prophylaxis and adherent, now 7 days post return with fevers and + malaria RDT.

parts.text: a) what is pathogen and where was it acquired?
b) Recommended treatment and 1 alternative
c) What are the advantages to this regimen
d) What should you monitor for?

cohort_answer.text:
Mefloquine-resistant P falciparum - Cambodia. (P vivax - Africa/Asia/South Pacific/Central-South America, possible but mefloquine resistance low unless Papua New Guinea; P ovale unlikely, endemic W Africa rarely SE Asia; P malariae exists in SEA but mefloquine sensitive/infrequent). RDTs: HRP2 targets P falciparum only, LDH and Aldolase pan-plasmodium
(Assuming NOT severe) Oral Artemisinin combination therapy (ACT); Malarone; Quinine + Clinda/Doxy. If severe: artesunate 2.4mg/kg 0,12,24,48hr + clindamycin or doxycycline or malarone; Alternative: Quinine 5.8mg/kg PLUS malarone/doxy/clinda
Mortality benefit with artesunate; oral/rectal options; dual treatment decreases treatment failure; less side effects; quicker drop in malaria load, kills all stages; low resistance rates
Parasite density typically daily until negative; if artesunate used, monitor weekly CBC for delayed hemolysis (up to 4 weeks after). Artesunate preferred: IV form, mortality benefit. Resistance suspected if recrudescence/parasite density does not drop

questions.question: Table of Malaria Diagnostics; Fill in 2 pros and 2 cons for Thin/Thick smear, RDT, PCR

parts.text: Fill in advantages and disadvantages for Thin/Thick smear, RDT (targets PfHRP-2 or pLDH), and PCR

cohort_answer.text: Thin/thick smear: advantage - quick, inexpensive, gives parasitemia level, can speciate; disadvantage - requires expertise, can miss low parasitemia. RDT: advantage - quick, no microscopy/specialized skills needed, small blood volume, simple, sensitivity 88-100%/specificity 92-95% for falciparum; disadvantage - false negatives (high parasitemia, low parasitemia <100/mL, P vivax, PfHRP-2 mutants), positive after treatment so can't assess response, inferior for P vivax detection, false positives with autoantibodies, heat/humidity sensitive, cross-reaction between species. PCR: advantage - very sensitive, detects low parasitemia, can speciate, can detect resistance; disadvantage - expensive, special equipment, trained technicians needed, no parasitemia level given

questions.question: 21. Malaria Treatment

parts.text: Adult with Uncomplicated vivax from Peru
Adult with Uncomplicated falciparum from Sudan
Adult with Complicated falciparum from Sudan
List 4 lab and 4 clinical criteria to diagnose severe Malaria

questions.model_answer: a) Uncomplicated vivax from Peru: chloroquine + primaquine (after G6PD testing) for radical cure. b) Uncomplicated falciparum from Sudan: artemether-lumefantrine (ACT). c) Complicated (severe) falciparum from Sudan: IV artesunate. d) Severe malaria criteria - Lab (4): parasitemia >5-10%, hypoglycemia, severe anemia (Hb <7 g/dL), acidosis/elevated lactate. Clinical (4): impaired consciousness/coma, seizures, respiratory distress/pulmonary edema, shock.

questions.question: Malaria Treatment: Adult with Uncomplicated vivax from Peru; Adult with Uncomplicated falciparum from Sudan; Adult with Complicated falciparum from Sudan; List 4 lab and 4 clinical criteria to diagnose severe Malaria

parts.text: Adult with Uncomplicated vivax from Peru
Adult with Uncomplicated falciparum from Sudan
Adult with Complicated falciparum from Sudan
List 4 lab and 4 clinical criteria to diagnose severe Malaria

cohort_answer.text: Vivax from Peru: Chloroquine phosphate 1g (600mg base) PO, then 0.5g in 6 hours, then 0.5g daily x2 days (total 5x500mg tablets) plus Primaquine 52.6mg (30mg base=2 tabs) PO daily x14 days. Uncomplicated falciparum from Sudan: Atovaquone-proguanil 4 tabs PO daily x3 days. Complicated falciparum from Sudan: Artesunate 2.4mg/kg q12h x4 doses. Severe malaria criteria - Lab: SCr>265, Anemia<70/HCT<20%, Glucose<2.2, Parasitemia>2% in non-endemic; Clinical: Altered LOC, Seizures, Jaundice, Respiratory Distress.

questions.question: P. falciparum malaria from Malawi was treated 10 days ago.

parts.text: What are 4 reasons the RDT could still be positive?
He's stable with no organ dysfunction, what is your suggested treatment?
What are 2 treatment recommended and with available regimens in Canada for uncomplicated P. falciparum

cohort_answer.text: Reasons RDT could still be positive: cure infected with persistence of antigens/DNA; persistent/relapsed infection; re-infection; positive rheumatoid factor (or non-specific heterophile antibodies). (RDT detects antigen - can remain positive even after parasite killed; would need thick and thin smear to assess parasitemia.) Suggested treatment (uncomplicated): Atovaquone-proguanil OR Quinine + Clindamycin/Doxycycline. Complicated malaria: IV Artesunate at 0, 12, 24, 48h, then at 52h start Malarone x3 days or Doxycycline/Clindamycin + Quinine x7 days. Pregnancy (CATMAT): Quinine + clindamycin; Hydroxychloroquine (cannot use primaquine in pregnancy).

questions.question: Q17 (2015). Man from Canada goes to India, then rural Cambodia to visit family. Takes mefloquine prophylaxis appropriately. Returns with fever, positive malaria screen.

parts.text: A) What is the pathogen and reason for fever?
B) What are 2 therapeutic options and which are preferred?
C) What are 2 advantages to the preferred therapy?
D) What follow-up tests do you need to do to ensure the therapy is working, not resistant?

cohort_answer.text: A) P. falciparum - chloroquine and mefloquine resistance in Thailand/Myanmar border, western Cambodia, Laos, southern Vietnam; preferred ppx in these regions would be Atovaquone-Proguanil or Doxycycline; mefloquine appropriate in India but not SE Asia. Alternate: dormant liver phase of P. vivax not killed by mefloquine, relapsed post-travel. Molecular markers: PfK13 (artemisinin resistance), Pfmdr1 copy number (mefloquine resistance), Pfcrt (chloroquine resistance), PfCytB mutation (atovaquone-proguanil resistance). B) Atovaquone-proguanil preferred due to fewer side effects than quinine (second option quinine+doxycycline); WHO preferred oral regimen artemether/lumefantrine (not available in Canada); if severe, artesunate preferred with parenteral quinine as alternative. C) Less side effects than quinine; more rapid fever/parasite clearance than quinine; reduced mortality in children/adults; active against broader life cycle range (gametocytes); no renal/hepatic dose adjustment; monitor for delayed hemolytic anemia with Hb at 7,14,30 days. D) Daily blood films/smears/parasitemia count; other bloodwork for complications - CBC, Cr, blood gas, glucose, lactate, bilirubin.

parts.text: Malaria table: name 2 advantages and 2 disadvantages of PCR, RDT, smear

questions.model_answer: PCR: Advantages - highest sensitivity/species-specific, detects low-level/mixed infections. Disadvantages - slow turnaround, not point-of-care, expensive. RDT: Advantages - rapid (15-20 min), no expertise required, point-of-care. Disadvantages - HRP-2 persists after cure (false positive), pfhrp2/3 gene deletions cause false negatives, less sensitive at low parasitemia. Thick/thin smear: Advantages - gold standard, quantifies parasitemia and speciates, low cost. Disadvantages - operator-dependent/requires experienced microscopist, time-consuming, insensitive at very low parasitemia if single smear only.

parts.text: Name 4-regimens for malaria prophylaxis in a traveler heading to Honduras including when to start and when to stop each drug

questions.model_answer: 4 regimens for malaria prophylaxis to Honduras (chloroquine-sensitive), with timing: (1) Chloroquine - start 1-2 weeks before travel, continue weekly, stop 4 weeks after leaving. (2) Atovaquone-proguanil - start 1-2 days before travel, continue daily, stop 7 days after leaving. (3) Doxycycline - start 1-2 days before travel, continue daily, stop 4 weeks after leaving. (4) Mefloquine - start 2-3 weeks before travel, continue weekly, stop 4 weeks after leaving.
questions.beyond_mandell: CDC Yellow Book malaria chemoprophylaxis timing recommendations.

questions.question: A youngish man was in Malawi and was diagnosed with Plasmodium falciparum. He was treated with artemether-lumefantrine. He was rechecked by his doctor in Canada 10 days later with a rapid diagnostic test and thick and thin smears. The rapid test was positive.

parts.text: What are four reasons why the test could be positive for this patient?
The thick and thin smears show only gametocytes on 2 of 3 smears. He is not planning on travelling anywhere for the next year. What do you tell him regarding treatment (2)?
What are 2 treatment regimens for uncomplicated malaria from this region that you could use? Medication options must be mutually exclusive.

questions.model_answer: a) Four reasons for persistent positive RDT: persistent HRP-2 antigenemia after cure, residual gametocytes, true recrudescence, or reinfection. b) With only gametocytes on smear and no further travel: no retreatment needed - gametocytes represent residual sexual-stage parasites, not ongoing/failed infection, and pose no transmission risk in a non-endemic setting without a competent vector; reassurance and clinical follow-up is appropriate. c) Two mutually exclusive regimens for uncomplicated falciparum from this region: artemether-lumefantrine OR atovaquone-proguanil.

questions.question: Returning traveler from 3 month stay in India, during which he took mefloquine. Fever, malaise, abdominal pain, hepatosplenomegaly, hypergammaglobulinemia, and hypoproteinemia.

parts.text: Diagnosis
Diagnostic procedure
Microbial agent
Treatment?

cohort_answer.text: Kala azar (visceral leishmaniasis). Diagnostic procedure: Splenic aspirate (sensitivity 96-98%); Bone marrow aspirate (sensitivity ~50%); Cultures from peripheral blood (buffy coat). Microbial agent: Leishmania donovani and L. infantum (synonym L. chagasi), transmitted by sandflies. Treatment: AmB 3mg/kg days 1-5, 14, 21 (only approved drug for VL).

parts.text: Why do you need to test for G6PD in P. vivax infection?
Describe the two proposed mechanisms of glucose metabolism alteration with fluoroquinolone antibiotics

cohort_answer.text: In P. vivax and P. ovale, the dormant hypnozoite liver stage needs to be eradicated; the 2 antimalarials with activity against hypnozoites are primaquine and tafenoquine, both of which can cause hemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency. FQ glucose mechanisms: stimulate release of insulin; interaction with hyperglycemic agents (e.g. glyburide).

questions.question: Malaria & Pregnancy. Pregnant woman at 6 weeks gestation going to Senegal.

parts.text: What advice would you give about malaria chemoprophylaxis?
She returns from her trip feeling unwell and febrile. What should you do?

cohort_answer.text: A) Pregnant travelers advised to defer travel to high risk areas until after delivery if feasible. Nonimmune pregnant women who cannot defer travel should take chemoprophylaxis; agents of choice chloroquine (chloroquine-sensitive areas, mefloquine also acceptable) and mefloquine (chloroquine-resistant areas). In this case mefloquine is the only ppx safe in pregnancy in Senegal (West Africa, known chloroquine-resistant malaria). B) Malaria thick and thin smear, RDT; blood cultures; assuming positive for falciparum, admit for monitoring; start artesunate IV; after 24-48h may transition to PO clindamycin +/- PO quinine x7 days. Artesunate has not been shown to cause harm to fetus and is first line for severe malaria in pregnancy.

questions.question: Q18 (2007). Pregnant woman with severe falciparum malaria

parts.text: A) Indications for exchange transfusion
B) Treatment
C) Are there any new treatments available only outside Canada?

cohort_answer.text: A) As per CATMAT, can be considered when parasitemia >10%. B) IV Artesunate 2.4mg/kg at 0h, 12h, 24h and 48h, follow with Clindamycin + Quinine PO x7 days. C) Artemether/lumefantrine x3 days; Tafenoquine (not for use during pregnancy because cannot assess fetal G6PD).

questions.question: 23F 6 weeks pregnant going to India / travelling to India. She returns from her trip with fevers/chills etc. What does the smear show (picture of a smear).

parts.text: What malaria ppx would you recommend?
She returns from her trip with fevers/chills etc. What does the smear show? How would you treat this infection?
What does the smear show?
How would you treat this infection?

cohort_answer.text: A) Mefloquine; advise against travel. Atovaquone/proguanil not recommended for pregnant women; region has chloroquine resistance so chloroquine cannot be used; doxycycline contraindicated in pregnancy; tafenoquine and primaquine not recommended in pregnancy/breastfeeding. B/D) If severe: Artesunate IV followed by artemether/lumefantrine (coartem) or clindamycin+quinine. If uncomplicated: PO artesunate 4mg/kg daily x3 days + mefloquine 25mg/kg; artemether-lumefantrine BID x3 days with food; dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine daily x3 days; quinine TID + clindamycin BID x7 days. Avoid artemisinin and derivatives during T1; avoid halofantrine, primaquine, tetracycline throughout pregnancy; avoid sulfadoxine near term; not enough evidence for malarone or coartem in pregnancy. C) P falciparum. Treatment (D): IV Artesunate 2.4mg/kg at 0h,12h,24h,48h, follow with Artemether/lumefantrine x3 days (if not in T1) or Clindamycin+Quinine PO x7 days.

questions.question: Q13. Returning Canadian traveller. Hb 65, SaO2 85%. Confused and GCS 9. Falciparum parasitemia 6%

parts.text: A) What criteria does he have for severe disease?
B) What is the histopathologic feature of cerebral malaria?
C) What are 4 other criteria for severe disease?

cohort_answer.text: B) Sequestration of infected erythrocytes in cerebral microvessels, 'ring' hemorrhages, perivascular leukocyte infiltrates, thrombin deposition, and activated platelets (Mandell's).

questions.question: Q14 (2009 PM). Malaria rapid detection test in a man who returns from Africa with fever. HRP assay is negative.

parts.text: A) 2 reasons why (presumably false negative)
B) Initial smear read as negative. Returns again and smear now shows 1% parasitemia with falciparum. TWO reasons why the initial smear was negative (other than lab error)

cohort_answer.text: A) The prozone effect (high dose-hook phenomenon) - false-negative/false-low results due to excess antigens or antibodies, blocking binding sites of detection/capture antibodies. B) Initial parasitemia below level of detection; parasite life cycle - parasites synchronize and trophozoites/schizonts can be sequestered in microvasculature.

questions.question: Q15 (2014, 2009 AM). Malaria - P. knowlesi

parts.text: A) How does it compare to other malaria species on thin smear?
B) What geographic area is it found?
C) Why is it relevant to distinguish it from other malaria species in the area?
D) How to identify on smear?

cohort_answer.text: A) P. knowlesi looks like P. malariae (though can have daily fevers and high parasitemia with knowlesi vs low parasitemia and fever q3days with malariae); blood stage (band-form) schizont indistinguishable from P. malariae; early trophozoite (ring shape) identical to P. falciparum. B) Mainly southeast Asia, majority from Malaysian Borneo; also Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, southern China, Vietnam, Laos, Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Andaman islands (India), Kalimantan, Sumatra, Indonesia - follows distribution of macaque hosts and Anopheles leucosphyrus vector. C) Associated with fatalities with delayed treatment; erythrocyte phase lasts 24h (shortest of any human malaria species), can develop daily fever spikes and rapid high parasitemia; severe disease in 6-9% of symptomatic adults.

questions.question: Q16 (2014). Malaria - define the endemic regions for: P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, P. knowlesi. What kind of malaria is in Papua New Guinea?

parts.text: Define the endemic regions and identify the malaria species in Papua New Guinea

cohort_answer.text: P. falciparum - widespread in nearly all malaria endemic areas: Sub-Saharan Africa, SE Asia/Papua New Guinea, upper South America (esp DR, Haiti), Oceania. P. vivax - Americas, West Pacific (Australia, New Guinea), Sub-Saharan Africa, India, SE Asia, upper South America (rare in central/western Africa due to Duffy negative phenotype); Florida and Texas recently locally acquired cases. P. ovale - Sub-Saharan Africa (esp west Africa) and Asia. P. malariae - sub-Saharan Africa, SE Asia, Indonesia, western Pacific islands, Amazon basin of S. America. P. knowlesi - SE Asia. Papua New Guinea: P. falciparum and P. vivax, chloroquine resistant (including P. vivax), mefloquine resistance.

parts.text: Why do you need to test for G6PD in P. vivax infection?

cohort_answer.text: P. vivax, P. ovale, or P. malariae infections require treatment of dormant hypnozoite liver stages with primaquine or tafenoquine to prevent relapse; both can cause oxidant hemolysis if G6PD deficient. Severe G6PD deficiency (5-10% normal activity): primaquine should not be used. ~20% G6PD activity: primaquine can be used at 0.75mg/kg qweekly x6 weeks, stop if significant hemolysis. Primaquine cannot be used in pregnancy because fetal G6PD status unknown.

questions.question: Q20 (2003 PM). Woman travels to Africa, doesn't take malaria ppx. Now has decreased LOC, blood film showing P. falciparum

parts.text: A) How would you treat this patient?
B) What are 5 signs of severe P. falciparum infection?
C) What adjunctive therapy can you suggest?

cohort_answer.text: A) Parenteral Artesunate 2.4 mg/kg (children <20kg: 3mg/kg) IV bolus over 1-2 min at 0, 12, 24, 48h; switch to oral follow-on after 24h if possible (if not, continue daily IV artesunate up to 7 days total); follow-on oral therapy starting 4h after final dose: Atovaquone-proguanil (adults 4 tabs daily x3 days with fatty food; peds 20mg/kg atovaquone + 8mg/kg proguanil daily x3 days) OR Doxycycline plus quinine sulphate OR Clindamycin (if unable to take doxy or atovaquone-proguanil) plus quinine sulphate. C) Supportive care; monitor BG q4h; respiratory support; treat seizures (benzos first line); fluid requirements target CVP 2-5cm (include dextrose); transfuse to target Hb>70 (>50 in high risk settings); manage concomitant bacterial infections; exchange transfusion can be considered if parasitemia >10% per CATMAT.

questions.question: Q21 (2006 PM). 23F 6 weeks pregnant, travelling to India.

parts.text: A) What malaria ppx do you recommend?

B) She returns from her trip with fevers/chills etc. What does the smear show (there is a picture of a smear, it was probably falciparum although there was a troph that looked rather vivax-like). How would you treat this infection?

cohort_answer.text: A) Drugs usable in pregnancy: Chloroquine (but resistance in India), Mefloquine. Cannot use: Primaquine, Tafenoquine, Malarone, Doxycycline. Answer given as: Mefloquine; advise against travel. B) If severe: Artesunate IV followed by artemether/lumefantrine (Coartem) or clindamycin. If uncomplicated: PO artesunate 4mg/kg daily x3 days + mefloquine 25mg/kg; Artemether-lumefantrine BID x3 days with food; Dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine daily x3 days; Quinine TID + clindamycin BID x7 days. Avoid artemisinin/derivatives in 1st trimester; avoid halofantrine, primaquine, tetracycline at all times in pregnancy; avoid sulfadoxine near term; not enough evidence for malarone or coartem in pregnancy.

parts.text: List 3 medications which can be used for malaria ppx in sub-Saharan Africa. Indicate dose, route, frequency and a contraindication (excluding hypersensitivity)

cohort_answer.text: Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) 250/100mg PO daily begin 1-2 days before travel until 7 days post-travel; contraindications: pregnancy, children <5kg, breastfeeding, CrCl<30. Doxycycline 100mg PO daily 1-2 days before travel until 4 weeks after return; contraindications: pregnancy, children <8 years. Mefloquine 250mg PO weekly from 2-3 weeks before travel until 4 weeks after; contraindications: hx seizures, psychiatric hx, cardiac conduction abnormalities; resistance at Thailand-Cambodian border and parts of China, Myanmar, Vietnam, Laos. Note tafenoquine avoid in pregnancy, psychiatric conditions, G6PD deficiency. Avoid chloroquine (high resistance in Africa).

questions.question: Q23 (2017 AM). Malaria ppx for travelers to Honduras

parts.text: Name 4 regimens. When to start and when to stop each drug?

cohort_answer.text: No resistance in Honduras. Malarone 250/100mg PO daily from 1-2 days before until 7 days after return. Doxycycline 100mg PO daily from 1-2 days before until 4 weeks after returning. Mefloquine 250mg salt PO weekly 3 weeks before until 4 weeks after returning. Primaquine 30mg PO daily from day 1 before to 7d after exposure (check G6PD first). Chloroquine 500mg salt PO weekly 1-2 weeks before until 4 weeks after travel (chloroquine sensitive areas: Mexico, Central America west of Panama Canal, Haiti, DR, Middle East - P. vivax, ovale, malariae, knowlesi). Tafenoquine begin daily x3 days prior (loading dose), weekly during travel, and 7 days after leaving.

questions.question: Q24 (2010 PM). Patient who presents after travel to West Africa with tachypnea and high fever, SOB, altered LOC, renal dysfunction, thrombocytopenia, anemia, crackles in chest. Smear shows P. falciparum, 2% parasitemia.

parts.text: A) What are 3 markers of severe malaria in this patient?
B) Assuming that you have access to all WHO recommended drugs, what are 2 recommended treatment regimens for this patient? Give first line and alternative option?
C) What oral drug would be used in addition to the options listed in b? Give drug name duration of tx

cohort_answer.text: A) Altered LOC; Respiratory distress; Anemia (Hct<15%?); AKI (Cr>250?). B) First Line: Artesunate IV 2.4mg/kg/dose at 0,12,24,48h. Alternate: Quinine IV loading dose 20mg/kg over 4h then 10mg/kg q8h. C) Artemisinin-based combination tx (artemether-lumefantrine) x3 days; Malarone (atovaquone/proguanil) with food 4 tabs daily x3 days; preferred oral regimens after ACT by WHO: Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x7days + quinine, or Clindamycin 20mg/kg/day PO div TID x7 days + quinine.

questions.question: Q25 (2018). 29yo patient, Canadian born, returns from West Africa with fever and dyspnea. GCS 9, SpO2 85%, RR 30, GCS 9, parasitemia 6%. (Alternate wording in 2018 peds exam: Kid travelled to Africa, presents with fever 39.5C, RR30, O2 sat 85%, parasitemia 6%, confusion/GCS 9.)

parts.text: A) What are 4 criteria for severe malaria met by this patient?
B) In general, what are 4 other criteria of severe malaria?
C) What is the histopathologic hallmark of cerebral malaria?

D) In the ideal circumstance, where all drugs are available to you, what drug and route of administration would you use to tx a patient with severe malaria (can't remember if they specified cerebral)?
E) IF the patient had a parasitemia of 2% on day 2, 1% on day 3, do you consider this to be an adequate response to therapy?

cohort_answer.text: A) Altered LOC; Parasitemia >5%; Respiratory distress; (not enough info given for 4th criterion). C) Dense sequestration of parasitized pRBC in CNS capillaries. D) IV Artesunate. E) Yes - after artemisinin tx, parasitemia clearance should be seen by day 5; if 1% by day 3 that is an adequate response; 6% likely underestimate given sequestration so 1% is a very good response. CDC: if after third IV artesunate dose parasite density >1%, continue IV artesunate once daily up to 7 days until density <=1%, then switch to oral regimen.

questions.question: Q43 (2018, 2009 AM, 2008, 2014). Returning traveler from 3 month stay in India, during which time he took mefloquine. Fever, malaise, abdominal pain, HSM, hypergammaglobulinemia, hypoproteinemia.

parts.text: A) Diagnosis?
B) Diagnostic procedure?
C) Microbial agent?
D) Treatment

cohort_answer.text: A) Kala Azar from visceral leishmaniasis, mostly Leishmania donovani or infantum; classic pentad prolonged fever, weight loss, HSM, pancytopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia; incubation 2-8 months. B) Clinical, parasitologic, immunologic dx: tissue (visualizing amastigotes), culture (visualizing promastigotes), PCR, Giemsa smear (direct smear from scraping/biopsy/tissue/fluid), Leishmania skin test (Montenegro). C) Leishmania donovani or infantum. D) Liposomal AmpB only approved for this indication 3mg/kg days 1-5, 14, 21.

questions.question: A patient returns from somewhere in Southern Africa. He was diagnosed with malaria while away and received Artemether-Lumefantrine. His family doctor notes a positive RDT. Creatinine and LFTs are normal.

parts.text: List 4 reasons why the RDT is positive.
A blood smear shows gametocytes on 2 of 3 smears. Do you treat and why?
2 recommended first line regimens if patient returning from Malawi for uncomplicated falciparum.

cohort_answer.text: Reasons for positive RDT: Persistence of gametocytes; persistent positive even after successful treatment (antibody-based can be positive ~30-60d post-treatment); re-infection or treatment failure; auto antibodies (RF); other non-plasmodium infection (African trypanosomiasis, toxo, TB, dengue). Gametocytes: No, do not treat - gametocytes will not cause symptoms; can consider treatment if in area with Anopheles mosquito to prevent disease introduction. First line regimens: Atovaquone-Proguanil (Malarone); Quinine + Clindamycin or Doxycycline.

parts.text: For each, list if you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): TB meningitis (0.5)
For each, list if you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): Neurocysticercosis with viable intraparenchymal cyst (0.5)
For each, list if you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): Cerebral malaria (0.5)
For each, list if you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): Acute schistosomiasis (0.5)
For each, list if you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): Large echinococcal cyst with risk of rupture during PAIR (0.5)

cohort_answer.text: TB meningitis - Yes, TB standards. Neurocysticercosis with viable intraparenchymal cyst - Yes, NCC guidelines. Cerebral malaria - No, associated with worse outcomes. Acute schistosomiasis - Yes, UTD/CDC. Also consider with neuroschistosomiasis. Large echinococcal cyst with risk of rupture during PAIR - No (no resources mention this). Additional notes: katayama fever (acute shisto) - yes (5 days of pred 40mg, followed by praziquantel per Mandell's); neurocysticercosis intraventricular lesions not calcified and no hydrocephalus - yes, dexamethasone 6-8mg/day divided TID for 28 days then slow taper over 2-8 weeks; not indicated in calcified cysts with isolated perilesional edema; steroids lower praziquantel levels and increase albendazole levels; TB meningitis - yes; non-HIV TB pericarditis can use steroids (not for pleural; if HIV+ insufficient evidence); ruptured echinococcus - no; cerebral malaria - no

questions.question: Trivia: Seven tropical infections that can be diagnosed with peripheral blood smear (Giemsa)

parts.text: Name the seven infections

cohort_answer.text: African/American trypanosomiasis, Babesia, Bartonella (bacilliformis - Oroya fever), Filariasis, Malaria, TBRF (tick-borne relapsing fever), LBRF (louse-borne relapsing fever) (also Histoplasmosis, Leptospirosis mentioned)

questions.question: List the vector (genus-level or common name) associated with the following infection:

parts.text: Dengue virus
Malaria
American trypanosomiasis
Endemic (murine) typhus

questions.model_answer: Dengue virus: Aedes mosquito (Aedes aegypti). Malaria: Anopheles mosquito. American trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease): triatomine ("kissing") bug. Endemic (murine) typhus: rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis).

parts.text: Dengue
Plasmodium falciparum
Trypanosoma cruzi
Endemic (murine) typhus

questions.model_answer: Dengue: Aedes mosquito. Plasmodium falciparum: Anopheles mosquito. Trypanosoma cruzi: triatomine ("kissing") bug. Endemic (murine) typhus: rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis).

questions.question: For each of the following, list if you would use steroids as adjunctive therapy (yes or no): TB meningitis; Neurocysticercosis with viable intraparenchymal cyst; Cerebral malaria; Acute schistosomiasis; Large echinococcal cyst with risk of rupture during PAIR.

parts.text: Indicate yes/no for steroid use in each scenario and rationale

cohort_answer.text: Katayama fever (acute schisto) - yes (5 days pred 40mg followed by praziquantel per Mandell's). Neurocysticercosis intraventricular lesions not calcified and no hydrocephalus - yes (dexamethasone 6-8mg/day divided TID for 28 days, then slow taper over 2-8 weeks; not indicated in calcified cysts with isolated perilesional edema; steroids lower praziquantel levels and increase albendazole levels, partial reason for albendazole use in limited CNS disease). TB meningitis - yes (non-HIV TB pericarditis can also use steroids, not for pleural; if HIV+ insufficient evidence). Ruptured echinococcus - no (not addressed in guidelines or UpToDate). Cerebral malaria - no

parts.text: Dengue virus
Falciparum malaria
Trypanosoma cruzi
